# Validation against the CLEAR corpus — 2026-08-29

**Every number in `eval/` before this one was generated by this repository and judged by a model.
This run scores prosemeter against 4,721 texts rated by roughly 1,800 human teachers.**

The formulas hold up. The product does not.

| what prosemeter returns | correlation with human ease | variance explained |
| --- | --- | --- |
| median-of-five grade (internal, not exported) | −0.527 | 27.8% |
| `grade-band` dimension score | 0.072 | 0.5% |
| composite | 0.235 | 5.5% |

The raw grade carries a real signal. The band score built from it does not, and the composite built
from that carries little. **The information is destroyed on the way out of the engine, not missing
from the engine.**

---

## The corpus

The CommonLit Ease of Readability (CLEAR) corpus: 4,724 excerpts, each with a `BT_easiness` score.
About 1,800 teachers each judged 100 **pairs** of excerpts for which was easier to read, and those
pairwise judgments were fitted with a Bradley-Terry model to give every text a continuous easiness
coefficient. Higher means easier.

That is the design run 7 amended itself toward — pairwise, many raters, aggregated — built at a
scale this repository was never going to reach by hand.

It is not vendored here. The data is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, and it is a 3.3 MB xlsx. Fetch it from
`github.com/scrosseye/CLEAR-Corpus`, then see "Reproducing" below.

3 of 4,724 excerpts fell below the 30-word floor `grade-band` requires and were dropped. n = 4,721.

## The method was validated before it was trusted

The corpus ships its own pre-computed formula columns, so the first thing to check is whether this
correlation code reproduces the published result.

**It does. CLEAR's own Flesch-Kincaid column scores −0.516 here against the −0.517 reported in the
paper.** Every other number below uses that same code path.

## 1. The formulas are competitive

| predictor | Pearson r | Spearman | R² |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CAREC (corpus's best) | −0.579 | −0.579 | 0.335 |
| SMOG | −0.562 | −0.571 | 0.316 |
| Dale-Chall | −0.557 | −0.597 | 0.310 |
| **prosemeter Flesch Reading Ease** | **0.553** | **0.569** | **0.306** |
| **prosemeter median-of-five grade** | **−0.527** | **−0.560** | **0.278** |
| Flesch-Kincaid | −0.516 | −0.547 | 0.266 |
| ARI | −0.484 | −0.518 | 0.234 |

**Taking the median of five formulas beats any one of them that prosemeter computes.** −0.527
against Flesch-Kincaid's −0.516 and ARI's −0.484. That is a small, real, externally-checkable
claim, and the first one in this repository that does not rest on its own generated corpus.

It is not the best available. CAREC, Dale-Chall and SMOG all beat it, and SMOG is already one of
the five being combined. A median is not the only way to pool them.

Worth noting for anyone reading the composite's weights: **the single best predictor prosemeter
computes is Flesch Reading Ease**, at 0.553, which the engine reports in a detail string and uses
for nothing.

## 2. The band destroys the signal it is built from

`grade-band` maps the median grade through a bidirectional band: 1 inside `[lo, hi]`, falling off
outside. That is deliberate, and the cost had never been measured.

**40.8% of the corpus — 1,925 of 4,721 excerpts — scores exactly 1.0.** Those excerpts span
`BT_easiness` from −3.59 to 1.71, against a full-corpus range of −3.68 to 1.71.

Two fifths of the corpus, covering 98% of the human difficulty range, is mapped to one number.

The dimension score correlates 0.072. The grade underneath it correlates −0.527.

This is not an argument against the band. A band is the right shape for "is this document in
range for its audience", and `LIB_ANLY_threshold-semantics_2026-08-07.md` already establishes why
a bidirectional target resists gaming. It is an argument that **the band should not be the only
thing exposed.** The median grade is currently unreachable except by regex over a detail string.

## 3. The composite is a floor, and the data says only a floor

Sorting the corpus into deciles by composite and reading the mean human easiness of each:

| composite decile | mean composite | mean `BT_easiness` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 68.5 | −1.805 |
| 2 | 73.8 | −1.192 |
| 3 | 78.0 | −0.697 |
| 4 | 81.3 | −0.817 |
| 5 | 83.8 | −0.877 |
| 6 | 85.6 | −0.934 |
| 7 | 87.2 | −0.754 |
| 8 | 88.6 | −0.916 |
| 9 | 90.2 | −0.840 |
| 10 | 92.8 | −0.753 |

**The first three deciles climb. Deciles 3 through 10 are flat** — every one of them sits at −0.8
give or take a tenth, in no order.

The composite separates badly-written text from everything else and then stops discriminating. It
is not a readability ranking above its bottom quintile.

That is exactly what `README.md` already claims — "a floor and a loop terminator, not a quality
oracle" — and this is the first evidence for it rather than an assertion of good faith. The claim
was right. It now has a number: R² 0.055, with the discrimination concentrated at the bottom.

## 4. Which dimensions carry readability

| dimension | r | R² |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `sentence-simplicity` | 0.485 | 0.236 |
| `clarity` | 0.152 | 0.023 |
| `grade-band` | 0.072 | 0.005 |
| `lexical-diversity` | 0.017 | 0.000 |

**`sentence-simplicity` is the one that tracks human judgment**, and nearly matches ARI as a
standalone predictor. That independently confirms what "What does not need re-testing" already
says from a different direction: it was the metric with a stable variance ratio across task sets,
and it is the metric with the strongest tie to human readers.

`clarity` at 0.152 is consistent with it being a document check rather than a readability measure.
`lexical-diversity` at 0.017 has no relationship with human readability on this corpus at all.

## 5. A calibration gap in the formula implementations

The corpus computes four of the same formulas independently, which makes this a differential test
against a published reference.

| formula | r | mean difference | max abs difference |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Flesch-Kincaid | 0.974 | **+0.56 grades** | 21.2 |
| Flesch Reading Ease | 0.984 | −2.74 | 55.6 |
| ARI | 0.972 | +0.37 | 27.1 |
| SMOG | 0.940 | +0.39 | 9.0 |

High agreement, with **a systematic offset: prosemeter reads text as about half a grade harder**
than the reference implementation. 5.7% of excerpts differ by more than 2 grade levels; 0.7% by
more than 5.

The largest disagreements are all long-sentence prose — a Robinson Crusoe passage chained with
semicolons, a Wilson peace-negotiation memoir, a Reformation article with a parenthetical Latin
gloss. Every one is a case where sentence boundaries are ambiguous, and in every one prosemeter
reads harder, which is what under-splitting produces.

**This points at sentence segmentation, not at the formula arithmetic.** It matters more than half
a grade sounds: the profile bands are tuned in grade units, so a systematic offset shifts what
falls inside every band in every profile.

## What this changes

- **Export the median grade.** It carries the signal the band score discards, and no public API
  returns it. This is the one clearly actionable result here.
- **Stop treating the composite as ordered above the bottom decile.** The floor framing in the
  README is correct and should be the only framing.
- **Investigate the segmentation offset** before any further band tuning. Bands calibrated against
  a splitter that disagrees with the reference by half a grade are calibrated against the splitter.
- **`sentence-simplicity` has now earned its weight twice**, by two unrelated methods.

## Limitations

- **The register is wrong for prosemeter's actual use.** CLEAR is literary and informational
  excerpts of 129–205 words, average publication year 1937.89. There are no READMEs, no API docs,
  no chat replies, no technical prose. These results validate `grade-band` on general English; they
  say nothing about the `readme`, `api-docs` or `chat` profiles on the documents those profiles
  target.
- **The ground truth is teachers rating difficulty for students in grades 3–12.** prosemeter's
  profiles mostly target adult technical readers. "Easy for a seventh-grader" and "clear to a
  senior engineer" are related but not the same quantity, and this measures the first.
- **Judging the band score by a linear correlation is unfair on its own terms.** It is designed to
  be non-monotonic, so a low r is partly a category error. The finding stands anyway, because the
  band score is what the product returns and 40.8% of documents land on the same value.
- **One corpus, one construction of the ground truth.** Bradley-Terry over pairwise judgments is a
  defensible aggregation and not the only one.
- **Nothing here measures the loop.** This is a static-scoring validation. Run 6 remains the only
  test of whether revision improves a document.

## Reproducing

The corpus is not vendored (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0). Two steps:

```bash
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/scrosseye/CLEAR-Corpus.git
python3 -m venv venv && ./venv/bin/pip install openpyxl
./venv/bin/python eval/clear-export.py CLEAR-Corpus/CLEAR_corpus_final.xlsx clear.jsonl

pnpm build
node eval/clear-correlate.mjs clear.jsonl
```

`clear-export.py` pulls the excerpt text, `BT_easiness`, and the corpus's own formula columns into
JSONL. `clear-correlate.mjs` scores every excerpt with prosemeter and prints every table above.
Scoring 4,721 excerpts takes about 47 seconds.

Source: Crossley, S. A., Heintz, A., Choi, J., Batchelor, J., Karimi, M., & Malatinszky, A. (2023).
A large-scaled corpus for assessing text readability. *Behavior Research Methods*.
